Location: RETURNING TO THE BONFIRE › Resting at The Bonfire (manuscript.md line 1906)
Current text: Resting at the bonfire also revives lost characters who have been removed from play due to dying while hollow.
Proposed fix: A character who dies while hollow is lost. A lost character's model is placed on its side beside the bonfire tile and takes no further part in the encounter. When a character is lost, the encounter is failed immediately and the characters must rest at the bonfire. Resting at the bonfire revives all dead and lost characters.
Rationale: The term 'lost' appears at lines 1890, 1906 and 2235 but is never defined. Death & Hollowing (1223) already forces an immediate rest when a hollow character dies, so 'lost' is a transient state that must be named once and added to the glossary.
Gameplay impact: Players cannot tell whether a lost character differs from a dead one or whether lost characters return after a free (post-boss) rest.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Objective & Loss Conditions (manuscript.md line 1201); Death & Hollowing (line 1223)
Evidence: manuscript.md:1201, 1223, 1253, 1341; DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt p.8 ('Once the dial reads 0 ... the next time a character is killed, the game is lost')
Current text: The players lose collectively if at any point, all characters are dead and there are no remaining sparks to revive them.
Proposed fix: When the characters are forced to rest at the bonfire and the spark dial shows zero, the players lose the game. The characters may not choose to rest at the bonfire while the spark dial shows zero.
Rationale: A hollow character's death fails the encounter while other characters are still alive (1305); the forced rest then costs a spark that does not exist, and the stated loss condition (all characters dead) never triggers. The official rule ties the loss to a death at zero sparks; the manuscript's forced-rest model needs the equivalent.
Gameplay impact: The game's only end-state for defeat has no rule that applies in the commonest defeat sequence.

Current text: Dropped souls are lost forever if the character who dropped them dies before reclaiming the souls.
Proposed fix: Souls dropped by a character remain on the encounter tile where they were dropped. Souls dropped at the moment of death are not forfeited by that death; they are returned to the supply only if the same character dies again before reclaiming them. When an encounter is failed, every living character drops their souls on that tile in addition to any souls already there. A character reclaims their own dropped souls only by surviving to clear the encounter on the tile where the souls lie.
Rationale: A hollow character's death simultaneously drops souls (1207) and fails the encounter (1305), so the literal text ('dies before reclaiming') forfeits the souls dropped by that very death. Line 1331 also makes all characters drop souls, including characters whose souls already lie on the tile. Hollowed Edition keeps dropped souls until a second death.
Gameplay impact: Whether a hollow character's death wipes their souls is the single largest soul swing in the game and is currently ambiguous.

Evidence: manuscript.md:1213, 1223, 1003
Current text: If any character survives to clear an encounter, then the characters who died in that encounter are revived in a hollow state.
Proposed fix: A character adventuring alone never becomes hollow: when that character dies, the encounter is failed and the character must spend a spark to rest at the bonfire.
Rationale: The revival branch requires a surviving character; a solo death therefore always falls to the failed-encounter branch, which costs a spark. Stating this explicitly removes the question of whether a solo character ever hollows.
Gameplay impact: Solo players need to know that every death costs a spark (the official 1E outcome).

Location: GAMEPLAY › Death & Hollowing (manuscript.md line 1221) vs Resting at The Bonfire (line 1898), Boss Death (line 2195), PvP (line 3046)
Current text: Hollow status is only removed by using a spark or an ember token.
Proposed fix: Hollow status is removed only by resting at the bonfire or by becoming embered.
Rationale: Resting after a boss (2195) and before PvP (3046) costs no spark yet removes hollow cubes (1898). The restriction must name the rest, not the spark.
Gameplay impact: Literal reading leaves characters hollow after the free post-boss rest.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Embering (manuscript.md line 1229) vs CHARACTERS › Ember (line 805) and CHARACTER TURN › Major Action › Ember (line 1834)
Current text: Ember: Place ember token on dashboard; discard equipped ember card.
Proposed fix: Ember (major action, or at any time outside an encounter): Discard an ember card from the back-up slot. Remove all damage cubes and all hollow markers from the endurance bar and place an ember token on the dashboard. The character is now embered.
Rationale: Three passages define embering; only Embering (1229) says it removes all damage cubes. A full heal as a major action is a major tactical resource and must be stated identically everywhere. Alternative: delete 'Remove all damage cubes' at 1229 so that embering only removes hollow markers (Hollowed Edition precedent, p.5).
Gameplay impact: Groups will disagree on whether embering heals; the difference is up to eight health in combat.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Embering (manuscript.md line 1243); Shop Rules (line 1949); Boss Death (line 2195)

Proposed fix: When a character becomes embered while holding an ember card, that character must immediately give the ember card to another character who is neither embered nor holding an ember card. If no such character exists, the ember card is returned to the tier one shop.
Rationale: Boss Death embers every character at once (2195), so a character holding an ember card is placed in an illegal state with no resolution. Alternative: return the card to the game box.
Gameplay impact: Rare but guaranteed to arise after the first boss when a character has bought an ember.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Encounters › Encounter Start step 2 (manuscript.md lines 1261–1263) vs CHARACTERS › Endurance Bar (line 787)
Current text: A character may never elect to spend excess stamina at the cost of receiving a staggered condition marker.
Proposed fix: The characters may skip cleared encounters only if every character can place all of the required stamina cubes without exceeding their endurance bar. A hollow character has six spaces. The stamina cubes for skipped encounters are placed at the start of the next encounter the characters fight.
Rationale: Skipping is elective, costs two stamina per skipped encounter per character, and a hollow character has six spaces; skipping four encounters (eight stamina) is therefore impossible under line 787, yet campaign sections list up to five encounters. Alternative: allow the skip and place a single stagger token for the overflow.
Gameplay impact: Determines whether hollow characters can use the skip mechanic at all in long sections.

Encounter Recovery lists stamina removal before condition removal, so a frostbitten survivor is blocked from the end-of-encounter recovery by the literal order.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Encounters › Encounter Turn Order step 3 (manuscript.md line 1291); ENEMY TURN › Enemy Movement (line 1672)

Location: SETUP › Character Setup step 7 (manuscript.md line 1001); Encounter Start step 8 (line 1275); Encounter Turn Order step 2 (line 1289)

Gameplay impact: Common with two characters of the same class family; cheap to fix.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Encounters › Encounter Turn Order step 3 (manuscript.md line 1291)
Current text: ...the character who placed the most damage tokens on enemy models.
Proposed fix: After all characters have taken their turns, place the aggro token on the character who inflicted the most damage on enemy models during that round, counting damage recorded on an invader's or boss's health dial as well as damage tokens.
Rationale: Invaders track damage on a dial, not with tokens; the literal measure excludes damage to invaders. The phrase 'that round' is also needed so that cumulative damage is not counted.
Gameplay impact: Prevents the aggro token ignoring the character fighting the invader.

Evidence: manuscript.md:1971–1993; DS-Phantoms-Rules-lores.txt p.6 (summons have taunt levels and block/resist/dodge values like characters), p.8–9 (weak-arc die, Distract icon, deck renewal)
Current text: Phantoms take their turn after all character turns are resolved and before the first enemy turn begins.
Proposed fix: A phantom is treated as a character for enemy targeting, range and node limits. A phantom never holds the aggro token unless a Distract icon on its behaviour card is resolved, in which case the phantom is treated as holding the aggro token until the end of the next boss turn. A phantom defends with the block, resist and dodge values on its data card, rolling dice as a character does. A phantom's health is not scaled. Phantoms gain the weak-arc black die. When a phantom's behaviour deck is empty, flip its discard pile face-down without shuffling.
Rationale: The manuscript gives a summoning procedure but none of the rules the Phantoms booklet supplies for how a summon is targeted, defends, interacts with aggro or renews its deck. A phantom with a health dial (1993) must be attackable, so targeting must be defined.
Gameplay impact: Boss behaviours cannot be resolved when a phantom is nearest or holds no defined aggro status.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Encounters › Encounter Start step 9 (manuscript.md line 1277); PLAYER VS PLAYER (line 3056)

Rationale: The first player token is not in the component list and is never used: character order is fixed by threat value (1289), so the token has no function. PvP calls the same object a 'First turn token'.
Gameplay impact: Removes a phantom component and a contradiction between two names.

Location: SUMMONS › Phantoms step 6 (manuscript.md line 1987) vs BOSS TURNS › Boss Turn Overview (line 2157)

Rationale: Phantoms are only ever summoned into boss encounters (1971), where boss and character turns alternate one at a time; 'after all character turns' has no meaning in that structure. The official rule is one phantom turn per character turn. Alternative: one phantom turn per full round of character turns.
Gameplay impact: Phantom activation frequency changes its value by a factor of up to four.

Location: BOSS TURNS › Boss Turn Overview (manuscript.md line 2157) vs Encounter Turn Order step 2 (line 1289)
Evidence: manuscript.md:1289, 2157
Current text: After each boss turn, one character may take their turn, then the boss takes another turn, a second character, and so-on.
Proposed fix: In boss encounters the players choose which living character takes each character turn, subject to the equal-turns rule. The descending threat order of ordinary encounters does not apply.
Rationale: Ordinary encounters fix character order by threat (1289); boss encounters say 'one character may take their turn', which implies free choice without saying so. Alternative: apply threat order in boss encounters as well.
Gameplay impact: Determines whether players can sequence the healer after the tank in boss fights.

Evidence: manuscript.md:1672, 1706, 1596; DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt p.25 (attack target icons, node icon, out-of-range miss, movement attacks); DS-TG-Rulebook p.25
Current text: Additional symbols beside the attack type icon modify the attack with special rules detailed later.
Proposed fix: An enemy attack targets the character shown by the small icon beside the attack icon: the skull icon targets the character with the aggro token; the ring icon targets the nearest character, with ties resolved as for enemy movement. If the target is not within the attack's range, the attack misses and has no effect. An attack with the node icon targets every character on the target's node; each targeted character defends separately. A push-movement that shows a damage value is a physical attack against every character on each node the enemy moves into, resolved separately for each character and defended as a normal attack.
Rationale: The promised 'special rules detailed later' never appear. Target selection, node (area) attacks and the out-of-range miss are defined only for movement, and the manuscript's push-movement paragraph (1594) never says that the damage number is an attack. Every enemy data card depends on these icons.
Gameplay impact: Enemy attacks cannot be resolved from the manuscript alone.

Location: COMBAT BASICS › Enemy Scaling (manuscript.md line 1529); Character Attacks › Repeat (line 1872); Boss Attacks (line 2187)
Evidence: manuscript.md:1529, 1579, 1872, 2187; DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt p.40 ('Repeat behaviour or attack' icon exists on official cards)
Current text: If playing with four characters, add repeat to each non-boss enemy's attack behaviour.
Proposed fix: When Repeat 2 is added by scaling, each attack icon on the enemy's data card is resolved twice in succession against the same target before the next icon is resolved. The damage value of a push-movement is not an attack icon and is not repeated. If an attack icon already bears a Repeat icon, increase its value by one.
Rationale: Repeat is defined for weapons (entire option) and bosses (entire card) but not for non-boss enemies, and official data cards already carry Repeat icons. Alternative: Repeat added by scaling does not stack with a printed Repeat icon.
Gameplay impact: Four-player games double or quadruple some enemy damage output depending on the reading.

Location: COMBAT BASICS › Enemy Scaling (manuscript.md line 1527); CAMPAIGN PLAY › Bonfire Ascetic (line 2342)

Rationale: Push-movement damage (1702) is a number inside a movement icon, not an 'attack value'; the scaling text does not say whether it is increased. Alternative: push-movement damage is never modified.
Gameplay impact: Trampling enemies (Sentinel, Smelter-type) are the ones where the +1 matters most.

Rationale: Literal reading of 1517 gives Base+2 for two characters; the table and line 1523 give Base+1.

Location: GAMEPLAY › Objective & Loss Conditions (manuscript.md line 1201) vs PLAYER VS PLAYER (line 3042)
Current text: Players may also choose to add a player versus player (PvP) encounter after the final boss is defeated ... / After each boss (mini, main, and mega) a PvP encounter will occur.
Proposed fix: If the players chose PvP during setup, a PvP encounter is played after each boss encounter (mini, main and mega) is cleared and before the characters rest at the bonfire.
Rationale: The objective text says PvP happens once, after the final boss; the PvP chapter says after every boss and its '+1 attack damage in future PvP' rule only makes sense with several PvP rounds. Alternative: a single PvP encounter after the final boss and deletion of the +1 rule.
Gameplay impact: Decides how many PvP rounds a game contains.

Current text: Character turn structure is unchanged from basic rules. ... Dodge difficulty is based on an the attacker attack option's stamina cost
Proposed fix: When a character attacks another character, the attacker resolves the attack option as if against an enemy and determines the final attack value. The defender then chooses to block, resist, dodge or parry exactly as against an enemy attack whose attack value equals that final attack value and whose dodge difficulty is given by the stamina-cost table. Damage suffered equals the attack value minus the defence total. Push, condition, shift and area-of-effect icons apply to characters as they apply to enemies; an area-of-effect attack targets every other character on the target node. A parry requires the attacker to share the defender's node; a successful parry staggers the attacker and permits a riposte. Block and resist values of defenders are never subtracted from the attack value; defence is always rolled.
Rationale: The PvP chapter supplies turn order, traps and a dodge table but never says how a character-versus-character attack is resolved: the enemy-attack procedure assumes a fixed attack value, the character-attack procedure assumes a fixed block value, and neither covers push, AoE, conditions or parry against a character.
Gameplay impact: PvP cannot be played from the text.

Evidence: manuscript.md:713, 967–981, 3062–3066; DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt p.18 (trap tokens show a dodge value and damage, or are blank)
Current text: Players place a trap token on an outermost available node after each turn. Characters that move onto a trap token may attempt to dodge. Characters that fail to dodge a trap immediately die.
Proposed fix: After each character turn, the player who took that turn draws a random trap token from the supply and places it face-up on an unoccupied outermost node (a node touching the tile edge) that holds no terrain or trap token; if no such node exists, the token is placed on any unoccupied node. A character who moves onto or is pushed onto a trap token rolls dodge dice against the trap's dodge difficulty; a blank token has no effect and is removed. On a failed dodge the character dies.
Rationale: Which player places the token, which token, whether it is face-up, what 'available' and 'outermost' mean, and how a trap's dodge difficulty is read are all unstated. The arena-shrinking effect is the only mechanism that ends a ranged stalemate, so it must work.
Gameplay impact: Without this the PvP end condition can never be reached between two cautious players.

Current text: Dead characters are excluded from PvP. ... Victory on non-final bosses provides +1 attack damage in future PvP only.
Proposed fix: The PvP encounter is played after dead characters have been revived and every character has been restored as if rested. A PvP encounter with fewer than two living characters is not played. Record a PvP victory by placing a 1-soul token from the supply on the champion's dashboard; in later PvP encounters the champion adds one to the attack value of every attack against a character.
Rationale: Clearing a boss revives the dead as hollow (1213) and PvP restores everyone (3046), so 'dead characters are excluded' is unreachable; and no marker is defined for the +1 bonus.
Gameplay impact: Removes an unreachable rule and gives the bonus a physical tracker.

Evidence: manuscript.md:3062–3076
Current text: The last character alive is awarded victory.
Proposed fix: If three consecutive rounds pass in which no character suffers damage, every character suffers one damage at the end of each further round until the encounter ends.
Rationale: Two ranged characters can retreat indefinitely; traps shrink the arena only slowly and a player may choose placements that never threaten themself. Alternative: rely on trap placement alone.
Gameplay impact: Guarantees termination of the optional mode.

Location: BOSS ENCOUNTERS › Character Arc Movement (manuscript.md line 2143)

Proposed fix: If a character is pushed off a boss's node, the character moves to a node adjacent to the boss's node within the same arc, chosen by the players. If no such node exists because of a wall or terrain, the character moves to any adjacent node touching that wall.
Rationale: 'Centre-most node' is undefined (arcs are wedges with no centre node on most tiles). The manuscript deliberately keeps the same-arc rule for pushes, which the FAQ relaxed; the simpler wording keeps that choice. Alternative: adopt the FAQ ruling (any adjacent node farther from the boss).
Gameplay impact: Frequent event in every boss fight.

Evidence: Defence total = two highest dice. With black dice the ceiling is 4 (2+2); mean of 2 black = 2.33, best-two-of-3 black = 2.88, best-two-of-4 black = 3.19. Official 1E (Core p.25) sums all dice (3 black mean 3.50). Combined with the Enemy Scaling table (L1519) this caps what any block build can absorb.
Current text: Determine the defence total by adding the number of sword pips on the highest two dice results. Additional dice beyond the two with the highest shown face value are ignored.
Proposed fix: Keep the rule but state the consequence in the Enemy Scaling section (see B-003/B-004) or raise the cap: "Determine the defence total by adding the number of sword pips on the highest two dice results. A shield adds its block dice to the pool and, if the character has a shield equipped, the three highest dice are used instead."
Rationale: Hollowed Edition p.7 introduced the two-dice cap to tame armour stacking, but it was paired with unscaled enemy attack values. The manuscript adds +1 attack at 3 players and Repeat at 4 players against the same cap, so damage leaks through on every hit at 3-4 players.
Gameplay impact: At 4 players a scaled Hollow Soldier (attack 5, Repeat 2) deals an expected 5.3 damage per activation to a 2-black-die blocker (see §2).

Evidence: Hollow Soldier (Core p.20: attack 4). At 4 characters: attack 5 with Repeat 2. Expected damage per activation vs 2 black block dice (best two) = 2 x 2.67 = 5.33 of an 8-box bar; P(kill full-health character in one activation) = 0.058; P(kill hollow character) = 0.444. At 1-2 characters the same enemy deals 1.67. Official 1E (Core pp.17-25) and V2 (p.16, player-count symbol = extra models) never add attack value or Repeat.
Current text: If playing with four characters, add *repeat to* each non-boss enemy's attack behaviour. [table: 4 | Base + 3 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | Repeat 2]
Proposed fix: Delete the Repeat row. Replace with: "If playing with four characters, increase each non-boss enemy's base health by one further point (Base + 4)." Table row 4: "4 | Base + 4 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -".
Rationale: Repeat doubles damage on top of the +1; with the two-highest-dice block cap no build can absorb it. A health step keeps the 4-player encounter longer without making single activations lethal.
Gameplay impact: 4-player expected damage per Hollow Soldier activation falls from 5.33 to 2.67; one-activation kill chance on a full bar falls from 5.8% to 0%.

Evidence: +1 attack at 3 characters raises Hollow Soldier expected damage from 1.67 to 2.67 (+60%) and removes the zero-damage block outcome (P(0) 0.111 -> 0). The health step (+1) is a +33% change at the same player count. Three characters also absorb three times the enemy activations of one character because all enemies act between every character turn (L1297-1311).
Current text: If playing with three or more characters, increase all non-boss attack values by one. [table: 3 | Base + 2 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -]
Proposed fix: "If playing with four characters, increase all non-boss enemy attack values by one." Table: row 3 "3 | Base + 2 | 1 -> 2 | - | -"; row 4 "4 | Base + 3 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -".
Rationale: Moves the attack step to the player count where the party has the most defensive redundancy and keeps each step of the table roughly equal in expected-damage terms.
Gameplay impact: 3-player encounters return to 1-2 player per-hit lethality while keeping +2 health per enemy.

Evidence: Skeleton Soldier (V2 p.24) has no attack icon; its only damage is a push attack inside its move. The rule adds Repeat to the 'attack behaviour'; it is undefined whether a push-move with damage counts, and the 2-player move 1 -> 2 rule already doubles that enemy's possible hits.
Current text: If playing with four characters, add *repeat to* each non-boss enemy's attack behaviour.
Proposed fix: If Repeat is retained: "Repeat applies to attack icons only. Movement behaviours, including push-moves that deal damage, are never repeated."
Rationale: Removes an ambiguity that otherwise quadruples push-mover damage at 4 players (two moves x Repeat 2).
Gameplay impact: Prevents a 2-damage push enemy becoming an 8-hit threat.

Location: L1511 vs L1523 (Enemy Data Cards vs Enemy Scaling)
Evidence: L1511 says scaled health = base + one per character 'in play'; L1523 says base + characters 'beyond one'. For 1 character these give base+1 and base respectively; the table (row 1 'Base Health') agrees with L1523.
Current text: When playing with more than one character, calculate a scaled health value by adding one health for each character (including dead characters) in play.
Proposed fix: "When playing with more than one character, calculate a scaled health value by adding one health for each character (including dead characters) beyond the first."
Rationale: Makes the two statements and the table agree.
Gameplay impact: Removes a one-health discrepancy at every player count.

Evidence: Tier Three 8 and Tier Four 8 are equal; every other cost progression is strictly increasing. The campaign table (L2303-2306) is exactly double the basic row for Tiers One-Three (4/8/16) and gives Tier Four 20, implying basic Tier Four = 10. Cumulative basic cost one stat: 2/6/14/22 as written, 2/6/14/24 with 10.
Current text: | Tier Four  | **8**           |
Proposed fix: | Tier Four  | **10**          |
Rationale: Preserves the author's own 1:2:4:5 ratio between the basic and campaign tables; 16 (doubling) would cost 30 cumulative, 68% of a character's whole-game income (44 souls), and would never be bought.
Gameplay impact: Tier Four costs 24 cumulative (55% of basic income) instead of 22; reaching it remains a deliberate end-game choice.

Location: L1391 (Souls) and Soul Reward Table L1401-1434
Evidence: "reward the reduced soul reward" is used but no reduced value appears anywhere in the manuscript. Candidate values: half rounded down 1/2/2/3 (re-clear of four tiles = 6-8 souls), half rounded up 2/2/3/3, reward-2 1/2/3/4 (campaign L1 would be 0), flat 1.
Current text: Upon successfully *clearing* an encounter that has been previously *cleared*, reward the reduced *soul* reward to each character.
Proposed fix: "Upon clearing an encounter that has previously been cleared, each character gains half the listed soul reward, rounded down." Add a third column to both Soul Reward Tables headed "Reduced reward": basic 1 / 2 / 2 / 3; campaign 1 / 1 / 2 / 2.
Rationale: Half-rounded-down is the strongest anti-grind value that still pays; a full four-tile re-clear (6-8 souls) is worth less than one Tier Three step (8), which matches the stated design goal of removing grinding.
Gameplay impact: Defines a rule that currently cannot be played; caps repeat income at about +14 souls per game.

Location: L1393 and L1415-1424 (Souls; Soul Reward Table row labels)
Evidence: L1393 says invaders give 'additional souls per player' without a number; the only figures are the row labels 'Standard Invaders 3' and 'Advanced Invaders 4' inside the encounter table. Official 1E gives 3 souls to the shared cache for any invader (Phantoms p.15), i.e. 0.75 per character at 4 players; the manuscript gives 3-4 per character, 4-5x the official reward.
Current text: Successfully defeated invaders provide additional *souls* per player.
Proposed fix: "A defeated standard invader provides three souls to each character; a defeated advanced invader provides four souls to each character, in addition to the encounter reward."
Rationale: States the figure in prose where the rule lives; the table alone is not a rule.
Gameplay impact: Confirms an invader is worth a whole extra encounter per character; acceptable given invaders act after every character turn (L2027).

Evidence: Solo start 6 souls (from Hollowed Edition p.2). Official 1E solo bonus is 16 souls in the cache (Core p.13) because one character carries every activation. Under the manuscript's unscaled 1-character enemies 6 souls = three tier-one cards or Tier One in three stats.
Current text: Characters adventuring alone start with six *souls* on their dashboard.
Proposed fix: No change required; if solo play tests as too hard, raise to ten souls.
Rationale: The reduced solo bonus is consistent with the manuscript's scaling (solo enemies are weakest).

Location: L2301-2306 with L2247-2280 (Campaign Stat Tier Costs and Campaign Soul Reward Table)
Evidence: First Journey (Core p.35 structure) under the campaign table yields about 55 souls per character over three sections; one stat to Tier Three costs 28 (51% of all income), Tier Four 48 (87%), four stats to Tier Three 112 (204%). The campaign both halves the per-encounter reward relative to level (2/3/4/5 vs 3/4/5/6) and doubles level costs.
Current text: | Tier Three | **16** | / | Tier Four | **20** | (campaign) and campaign rewards 2/3/4/5
Proposed fix: Keep the campaign reward table at the basic values (3 / 4 / 5 / 6) and retain the doubled stat costs; or keep 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 and set campaign Tier Three to 12 and Tier Four to 16.
Rationale: Two simultaneous halvings make a three-session campaign end with most characters at Tier Two in one stat, below where the basic game ends after one session; one lever is enough to slow progression.
Gameplay impact: With basic rewards the campaign total rises to about 73 per character: one stat to Tier Three plus a second to Tier Two plus two tier-two cards, i.e. one full tier beyond the basic game across three sessions.

Location: L1197 (Objective & Loss Conditions) with L1223 and L1341 (forced rest)
Evidence: A failed encounter 'forces' the party to spend one spark and rest. The loss condition only triggers when all characters are dead and no sparks remain. The state 'hollow character dies, survivors standing, spark dial at 0' is undefined: the forced rest cannot be paid. Spark budgets: 4 players have three paid rests in the whole basic game.
Current text: The players lose collectively if at any point, all characters are dead and there are no remaining sparks to revive them.
Proposed fix: "The players lose the game when an encounter is failed and the spark dial shows zero."
Rationale: A failed encounter always demands a spark; defining the loss at that moment closes the gap and matches official 1E (Core p.8: once the dial reads 0, the next time a character is killed the game is lost).
Gameplay impact: Makes the end state deterministic; no numeric change.

Evidence: Campaign maximum = starting sparks (4 players: 2). A boss defeated at a full dial gives nothing. Adding a fourth player to a three-player party holding 1 spark leaves 0 sparks with a maximum of 2. Official 1E campaign (Core p.33) allowed buying a spark for 2 souls per character up to the maximum; the manuscript forbids any purchase.
Current text: The starting number of sparks also serves as the maximum number of sparks. ... Sparks cannot be purchased or gained otherwise. ... New players can join a campaign that is in progress at the cost of one spark each.
Proposed fix: "The maximum number of sparks is the starting number plus one. While resting at the bonfire the characters may buy one spark for four souls per character, up to the maximum. A new player may join only while the spark dial shows at least two."
Rationale: Restores the official pressure valve at double the official price (consistent with the manuscript's doubled prices) and removes the two degenerate states.
Gameplay impact: A four-player campaign can hold up to 3 sparks and can convert about 16 souls into a rest when a section goes badly.

Location: L1261-1263 (Encounter Start step 2) with L781 and L791-795
Evidence: Three skipped encounters = 6 stamina (the manuscript's own example). Hollow bar = 6 spaces, so a hollow character starts with zero free boxes: any damage kills (L795) and any stamina cost is forbidden (L791-793), leaving Rest as the only legal major action. A healthy character with three skips has 2 free boxes: P(death) from one Hollow Soldier hit (attack 4, 2 black block dice) = 0.556; at 3 players (attack 5) 0.889. Any hollow death fails the encounter and costs a spark (L1223).
Current text: Characters may skip previously *cleared* encounters at the cost of two stamina cubes placed in the endurance bar of each character. For example, if the first three encounters are marked *cleared* then the characters could skip to the fourth encounter but would all start with 6 stamina expended.
Proposed fix: "Characters may skip previously cleared encounters. Each character places one stamina cube in their endurance bar for each encounter skipped, to a maximum of three. For example, if the first three encounters are marked cleared, the characters may skip to the fourth encounter and each starts it with three stamina spent."
Rationale: The skip is a time-saving device; the tax must leave a hollow character at least three free boxes (6 - 3 = 3) so that the first enemy phase is survivable.
Gameplay impact: Hollow three-skip death chance per Hollow Soldier hit falls from 100% to 19% (3 free boxes, attack 4); healthy from 56% to 3%.

Evidence: Manuscript: endurance bar 'total of eight stamina/damage cubes', hollow reduces to six. Official 1E boards have ten boxes (Core p.20: 'If all ten of a character's endurance bar boxes have cubes'; Herald board image p.11). Hollowed Edition p.5 applies the same two cubes to the official ten-box bar. Every survivability figure in B_report assumes eight.
Current text: The effect of these *hollow* markers is to reduce the functional capacity of the endurance bar from a total of eight stamina/damage cubes to only six.
Proposed fix: Either (a) "from a total of ten stamina and damage cubes to eight" if official dashboards are used, or (b) state in Game Components that Second Edition dashboards have an eight-space endurance bar.
Rationale: The number must match the physical component the players own; nothing in the manuscript announces new dashboards.
Gameplay impact: Two boxes = 25% of capacity; with ten boxes the 4-player Repeat Hollow Soldier one-activation kill chance drops from 5.8% to 0.1%.

Evidence: Threshold = highest requirement + 10. Tier-two weapons (requirement >= 25) need a stat >= 35; the highest Tier Four value is 40 (Core p.33) or Tier Three + 5 (L1914: Herald STR 42, DEX 39, INT 34, FTH 45). Only weapons with requirement <= 30 (STR/FTH) or <= 29 (DEX) can ever scale, and only at Tier Four; tier-one weapons scale at Tier Two-Three (Mace 16 -> STR 26 at Herald Tier Two 28; Rapier 21 -> DEX 31 at Tier Three 34). Uchigatana (32), Falchion (37), Dragon Tooth (40) can never scale.
Current text: If the character's current stat value exceeds an equipment's highest stat requirement by ten or more points, the character should mark the equipped item with a red damage cube to indicate that it is scaled.
Proposed fix: "If the character's current stat value exceeds the equipment's highest stat requirement by five or more points, mark the equipped item with a red damage cube to indicate that it is scaled."
Rationale: A ten-point margin rewards keeping tier-one weapons into the end-game and excludes almost every tier-two weapon; five points lets a Tier Three or Four character scale the weapons the tier-two deck is meant to deliver.
Gameplay impact: Uchigatana scales at DEX 37 (Tier Four), Carthus Curved Greatsword at DEX 35; tier-one weapons are unchanged in practice (Mace needs STR 21, still first reached at Herald Tier Two 28).

Evidence: Manuscript: Tier Four = Tier Three + 5 (Herald FTH 45, INT 34). Official 1E campaign: 'The value of any stat at Tier 4 is considered to be 40' (Core p.33); Hollowed Edition p.3: 'sets the attribute to 40 stat-points, i.e. the maximum'. The highest requirement in the manuscript's weapon table is 40 (Dragon Tooth). Under '+5' a Herald INT Tier Four (34) cannot equip a 35-requirement item that a '40' rule would allow; under '40' a Herald FTH Tier Four equals Tier Three (40) and buys nothing.
Current text: Tier four stats are all considered 5 greater than the tier three stat value.
Proposed fix: "A stat at tier four is treated as 40, or as five greater than its tier three value if that is higher."
Rationale: Keeps the official value, guarantees Tier Four is always an improvement, and makes every printed requirement (max 40) reachable.
Gameplay impact: Herald Tier Four: STR 42, DEX 40, INT 40, FTH 45.

Evidence: Falchion 37/30: the second-highest STR requirement of the 60 rows (only Dragon Tooth 40 is higher), above Black Knight Greataxe 32 and Vordt's Great Hammer 33, for a basic one-handed curved sword. The stated method (L3210) raised a primary stat 'to ensure overall balance remained roughly equal'; 37 is not roughly equal to any plausible original.
Current text: Falchion 37 30 0 0
Proposed fix: Falchion 17 30 0 0
Rationale: A digit transposition (17 -> 37) is the most economical explanation; 17/30 keeps the weapon tier two on DEX, consistent with Scimitar 18/20 and Shotel 26/29.
Gameplay impact: Makes the Falchion equippable by a DEX character at Tier Two-Three instead of requiring STR Tier Three/Four.

Location: L3226-3228 (Carthus Curved Greatsword 19/30; Carthus Curved Sword 25/35)
Evidence: The greatsword requires less of both stats than the one-handed sword; every other paired weapon in the table (Mace/Great Mace, Claws/Manikin Claws, Halberd family) has the heavier weapon higher. STR 25 also pushes the one-handed sword into tier two by one point.
Current text:
Carthus Curved Greatsword 19 30 0 0
Carthus Curved Sword 25 35 0 0
Proposed fix:
Carthus Curved Greatsword 25 35 0 0
Carthus Curved Sword 19 30 0 0
Rationale: Swapping the two lines restores the heavier-weapon-higher ordering without introducing new values.
Gameplay impact: Both remain tier two; the one-handed sword becomes reachable at DEX Tier Two-Three.

Location: L3222 (Butcher Knife 25/0), L3236 (Dark Silver Tracer 0/25), L3324 (Warden Twinblades 17/25)
Evidence: Three rows sit exactly on the 25 split with their only or highest requirement; one point decides which deck they enter. Twelve rows in total are within two points of the split (see B_report §8.1).
Current text: Butcher Knife 25 0 0 0 / Dark Silver Tracer 0 25 0 0 / Warden Twinblades 17 25 0 0
Proposed fix: Decide each boundary row deliberately and move it off the split: Butcher Knife 24 0 0 0 (tier one) or 28 0 0 0 (tier two); Dark Silver Tracer 12 26 0 0; Warden Twinblades 17 26 0 0.
Rationale: A tier boundary that coincides with a requirement is read differently by every table; the manuscript's own threshold phrase ('equal or greater than 25', L1013) must then be checked card by card during setup.
Gameplay impact: Deck composition changes by at most three cards.

Location: L3232 (Claws 0/20), L3270 (Manikin Claws 24/24), L3280/L3290 (Parrying Dagger = Rapier 14/21), L3224 (Caestus 0/15)
Evidence: Claws and Manikin Claws are the same weapon class 24 STR apart; Parrying Dagger and Rapier are identical; Caestus, Claws, Throwing Knives, Dark Silver Tracer and Priscilla's Dagger keep STR 0 although the rationale (L3210) says zero requirements were replaced. Nine identical stat lines exist in the table (B_report §8.1).
Current text: Claws 0 20 0 0 / Manikin Claws 24 24 0 0 / Parrying Dagger 14 21 0 0 / Rapier 14 21 0 0 / Caestus 0 15 0 0
Proposed fix: Claws 12 20 0 0; Manikin Claws 14 24 0 0; Parrying Dagger 10 18 0 0; Caestus 12 10 0 0. Add a sentence under the table: "A requirement of 0 is intentional where shown." for any row left at zero.
Rationale: Brings the rows into line with the method the section states; distinguishes main-hand from off-hand tools.
Gameplay impact: All affected rows remain tier one.

Location: L1069/L1079/L1085 (Shop Setup) with L823-829 (Equipment Cards), L747-753 (Equipment Slots), L1769 (Parry)
Evidence: The stock list requires '2 shields' per shop and the parry rule requires 'a shield as their left weapon', but the card-typing rules define only one-handed weapon, two-handed weapon, armour (by icon) and spell (by scroll art). No rule says how a shield is recognised; shields are weapon-typed cards in 1E (East-West Shield appears in the manuscript's own weapons table, L3244).
Current text: Equipment cards include weapons, spells, shields, armour, and items which the character equips to improve their combat capabilities. ... 3 weapons, 3 armour, 2 shields, 2 upgrades, and 2 spells.
Proposed fix: Add to Equipment Cards: "A shield is a one-handed weapon card that shows a block or resist value and has no attack option. Shields count as weapons for equipment slots and as shields for shop stocking and parrying."
Rationale: The shop and parry procedures cannot be executed without a test for 'shield'.
Gameplay impact: Makes the 12-card stock list and the parry prerequisite determinable.

Evidence: Filling 3/3/2/2/2 by drawing one card at a time needs about 22-28 draws from the tier-one deck under an assumed type mix (weapons 45%, armour 20%, shields 10%, upgrades 12%, spells 13%); the 2-shield quota is the bottleneck (P(<2 shields in 20 draws) = 0.39) and the tier-two deck may hold too few upgrades (Titanite Shards are tier one) to fill '2 upgrades' at all. About 15 drawn cards are reshuffled back each stocking.
Current text: Draw tier one treasure cards one at a time to stock tier one shop: 3 weapons, 3 armour, 2 shields, 2 upgrades, and 2 spells. ... Reshuffle extra treasures back into the tier one treasure deck.
Proposed fix: "Draw cards one at a time until every category is filled or twelve cards have been drawn, whichever comes first. Place each card in its category if that category is not yet full; otherwise set it aside. Categories still unfilled after twelve draws remain empty. Shuffle the set-aside cards back into the deck."
Rationale: Bounds the setup time and handles decks that cannot supply a category.
Gameplay impact: Shop may open with fewer than 12 cards in rare cases; expected stocking time roughly halves.

Location: L3082-3094 (Player vs Player, dodge difficulty table)
Evidence: Table [0]->4, [1]->3, [2]->2, [3]->1, [4]->1, [5+]->0. With green dice at p = 0.5, difficulty 4 is impossible with fewer than four dice (P = 0.062 with four); difficulty 3 is impossible with two dice. Free and 1-stamina options (the weakest attacks on most cards, e.g. Shortsword [0] 2 black, Core p.22) become the hardest to avoid, while [5+] attacks are dodged automatically. [3] and [4] share the same value.
Rationale: Keeps the intended inversion (cheap attacks harder to dodge) within the range the dice can produce and removes automatic outcomes in either direction.
Gameplay impact: A two-dice defender dodges a free attack 25% of the time instead of 0%; a 5-stamina attack is dodged 50-94% instead of always.

Evidence: Each poison token deals 1 damage at end of activation and only one token is removed, so n tokens inflict n + (n-1) + ... + 1 damage: 2 tokens = 3, 3 tokens = 6, 4 tokens = 10 (more than a full 8-box bar). Official 1E/V2: 1 damage per activation (V2 discards the token). Hollowed p.8 consumes all tokens at once for n damage.
Current text: *Poison* tokens are not limited to one per model. A model suffers one damage for each *poison* token it has at the end of its activation, then removes only one *poison* token.
Proposed fix: "Poison tokens are not limited to one per model. At the end of its activation a model suffers one damage for each poison token it has, then removes all of its poison tokens."
Rationale: Adopts the Hollowed Edition value the manuscript otherwise follows; stacking remains meaningful (n tokens = n damage) without triangular growth.
Gameplay impact: Three poison hits deal 3 damage instead of 6.

Evidence: Manuscript: -1 to block, resist and dodge results, not removed until the encounter ends. Official (DS-BDK-Rules-web, text lines 452-458): -1 success on the roll; the token is removed when the character suffers damage from the attack. Per-hit cost with 2 black block dice is +0.97 expected damage; over a five-hit boss fight the persistent version costs about +4.9 damage against about +1 for the official version.
Current text: *Calamity* tokens are not removed at the end of a model's turn. *Calamity* tokens are only removed at the end of the encounter.
Proposed fix: "Calamity tokens are not removed at the end of a model's turn. A Calamity token is removed when the affected model suffers damage from an attack."
Rationale: Restores the official duration; Kalameet already applies the token repeatedly (BDK: Mark of Calamity is always in the deck).
Gameplay impact: Reduces Kalameet's effective damage by roughly 4 per fight per character.

Evidence: 7 x 4 (poison, bleed, stagger, frostbite) + 4 x 2 (calamity, corrosion) = 36, not 35. Core set supplies 5 of each basic condition (Core p.7) = 20; BDK supplies 4 Calamity.
Current text:
- 35x Condition tokens
  - 7x each of poison, *Bleed*, *Stagger*, and frostbite tokens
  - 4x each of *Calamity* and *4x Corrosion* tokens
Proposed fix:
- 36x Condition tokens
  - 7x each of poison, bleed, stagger and frostbite tokens
  - 4x each of calamity and corrosion tokens
Rationale: Sum must equal the itemised list; the stray '4x' inside the second sub-item is removed.

Location: L683 (Soul tokens) with L1383 (Souls are individual)
Evidence: Supply 10x1 + 5x3 + 3x5 + 1x8 = 19 tokens, total face value 48 (the Core set's shared-cache supply, Core p.7). The manuscript makes souls individual and non-transferable; four characters each holding 15-20 souls (B_report §4.2) need 60-80 in face value.
Current text: - 10x1, 5x3, 3x5, and 1x8 Soul tokens
Proposed fix: Add after the token list: "Soul tokens are not limited. If the supply runs out, use any convenient counters or record souls on paper."
Rationale: Individual soul tracking exceeds the printed supply in ordinary play.
Gameplay impact: Avoids an artificial cap of 48 souls across the party.

Location: L689 (Stat tier cubes) with L781, L1215, L1367 (hollow markers 'white cubes')
Evidence: 16 white cubes = 4 characters x 4 stats, all placed on dashboards at setup (L771). Hollow status is marked with two white cubes per hollow character; in a four-character game none are spare.
Current text: When a character dies and is revived *hollow*, they block off the two furthest right spaces of the endurance bar with a marker such as white cubes.
Proposed fix: "...block off the two furthest right spaces of the endurance bar with two hollow markers (use the Tier Four red cube from a stat track that has not reached tier four, or any two counters)." and add "8x Hollow markers" to the component list.
Rationale: A marker must exist in the component list; white cubes are fully committed at four players.

Location: L1277 (Encounter Start step 9) and L3058 (PvP 'First turn token') vs component list L681-716
Evidence: A 'first player' token (and in PvP a 'First turn token') is used but not listed among components. Core p.7 lists '1x First Activation Token'.
Current text: 9.  Place the *first player* token on the character with the highest threat value.
Proposed fix: Add "1x First player token" to Tokens & Terrain Elements; use the term "first player token" in both the Encounter Start and Player vs Player sections.
Rationale: Component used in play must be listed; one term throughout.

Evidence: 'This effect is cumulative with stat scaling for character count.' Hollow Soldier (Core p.20, attack 4) in a 4-character campaign after the Ascetic: attack 6 with Repeat 2. Expected damage per activation vs 2 black block dice = 2 x 3.67 = 7.33 of an 8-box bar; P(kill a full-health character in one activation) = 0.444; P(kill a hollow character) = 0.914. An icon-key 5-attack enemy (Core p.25) becomes 7 x2 = 9.33 expected, lethal to a full bar on average. At 3 characters: attack 6, 3.67 per activation.
Current text: After the bonfire ascetic has been burnt, all non-boss enemies increase their attack damage by one for the remainder of the campaign. This effect is cumulative with stat scaling for character count.
Proposed fix: "After the bonfire ascetic has been burnt, all non-boss enemies increase their base health by two for the remainder of the campaign. This increase is cumulative with the health scaling for character count. Enemy attack values are not changed."
Rationale: A second +1 attack on top of player-count scaling pushes every ordinary enemy past what the two-highest-dice block cap can absorb; a health increase lengthens fights without making single activations lethal and matches the 'stronger enemies' flavour.
Gameplay impact: 4-player post-Ascetic Hollow Soldier: health 6 instead of 4, expected damage per activation 2.67 (if B-003 is adopted) instead of 7.33.

Location: L1477 (Treasure Rewards, crystal lizards) vs L2057 (Crystal Lizards)
Evidence: L1477 awards 'a Titanite Chunk card' for killing a crystal lizard; L2057 awards 'one Titanite Scale card'. Official Iron Keep rules (text lines 125-131) award a Titanite Scale; the manuscript's own errata list (L3126) redefines Titanite Chunk as a +2 upgrade that must replace a Shard.
Current text: If playing with the option of *crystal lizards*, award a Titanite Chunk card to any character who killed a *crystal lizard* during the encounter.
Proposed fix: "If playing with the option of crystal lizards, award one Titanite Scale card to any character who killed a crystal lizard during the encounter."
Rationale: One reward name across both sections, matching the component list of the Iron Keep expansion (3x Titanite Scale cards).
Gameplay impact: Prevents the +2 Chunk (a stronger upgrade) being handed out for an optional side-kill.

Evidence: Two extra stamina buy one extra green die (p = 0.5). Against dodge difficulty 2 (Hollow Soldier, Core p.20) a two-dice character rises from 0.25 to 0.50; expected damage avoided = 0.25 x 1.67 = 0.42 for 2 stamina, which also buys a full Shortsword [2] attack (3.50 raw). Against difficulty 1: 0.75 -> 0.875.
Current text: Characters may spend two additional stamina (total of three stamina cost) before rolling dice to add a single additional *dodge* die to their roll, up to a maximum of four *dodge* dice.
Proposed fix: "Characters may spend one additional stamina (total of two stamina) before rolling dice to add a single additional dodge die to their roll, up to a maximum of four dodge dice."
Rationale: At 2 extra stamina the option is almost never worth taking; at 1 it is a real decision.
Gameplay impact: Dodge-build characters gain an affordable emergency option; expected stamina spent on dodging rises slightly.

Location: L2316, L2334, L2338-2340 (Bonfire Ascetic cost 16 shared)
Evidence: 16 souls shared by 3 characters = 5.3 each, about 10% of the First Journey campaign income of ~55 per character; the party can burn the Ascetic during section 1 (17 souls per character earned) before any equipment upgrade, immediately triggering +1 enemy attack for the rest of the campaign.
Current text: Characters may pay a communal one time fee to burn the bonfire ascetic to gain access to tier two treasures. A total of sixteen souls may be paid from any combination of character contributions while resting at the bonfire.
Proposed fix: "Characters may pay a communal one-time fee of eight souls per character to burn the bonfire ascetic and gain access to tier two treasures. The ascetic may be burnt only after the final boss of the first section has been defeated."
Rationale: Scales the fee to party size (a fixed 16 is 16 for a solo character but 4 each for four) and prevents the difficulty increase arriving before the party can use tier-two cards.
Gameplay impact: Solo campaign pays 8 instead of 16; four-player campaign pays 32 instead of 16.

Location: L2047-2049 (Mimics) with L1455-1463 (Treasure Rewards, mimic ambush)
Evidence: Characters 'do not recover stamina, remove damage ... until a decision is made' and then fight the mimic (Hungry Mimic health 18, heat-up 8, deck 4; Explorers text) from their end-of-encounter nodes with the stamina and damage they carry. After a 4-character scaled encounter this is typically 4-6 stamina and 2-4 damage already on an 8-box bar; the mimic acts first and needs about six activations to kill with starting weapons.
Current text: Characters remain on the nodes they occupied at the end of the encounter containing the chest. The mimic will take its turn first.
Proposed fix: "Characters remain on the nodes they occupied at the end of the encounter containing the chest and remove all stamina cubes, but no damage cubes, before the mimic takes its first turn."
Rationale: Keeps the ambush dangerous (damage carries over) without starting the fight with characters unable to act.
Gameplay impact: Mimic fights begin with full stamina; expected character deaths in the first mimic activation fall sharply at 3-4 players.

Location: L1531 (Enemy Scaling: bosses do not scale) with L2184 (Boss Turn Overview)
Evidence: Boss health is fixed (consistent with Core p.26 and V2 p.28). Because the boss acts after every character turn, the number of boss activations needed to kill it is independent of player count (example boss 24 health / block 2: about 11 character turns with Shortsword [2], 6 with tier-two weapons), so each character absorbs 1/N of the boss's attacks. Combined with the ordinary-encounter scaling of L1519-1560, the route is harder than the boss at 4 players and easier than the boss at 1 player.
Current text: Boss enemies (mini, main, and mega) do NOT modify their base health or receive scaling benefits otherwise.
Proposed fix: No change to the boss rule; adopt B-003/B-004 so that encounter difficulty does not invert relative to bosses. Optionally: "At four characters, increase a mini-boss's or main-boss's starting health by four."
Rationale: Both official editions leave bosses unscaled; the inversion is caused by the encounter table, not by the boss rule.
Gameplay impact: None unless the optional sentence is adopted (adds about two boss activations at 4 players).

Evidence: Bleed: 3 unblockable damage on the second token (Hollowed p.8) vs official +2 when next damaged (Core p.21, V2 p.21): 3 damage = 37.5% of an 8-box bar, and two bleed hits kill any enemy with scaled health <= 3 outright. Stagger -1 to dodge turns a one-die dodger into an automatic failure. Both are deliberate departures and internally consistent.
Current text: If a second *bleed* token would be placed on a model, deal three damage and remove all *bleed* tokens from that model. ... *Staggered* models subtract one from *attack*, *block*, *resist*, and *dodge*.

Rationale: The strongest condition in the game needs an explicit boss ruling; the values themselves are a reasonable design choice.
Gameplay impact: Clarifies whether bleed weapons are the best anti-boss tool.
